planting.note: Set container transplants in spring into a gritty, sharply drained scree or crevice mix; seed is slow and needs a long cold stratification, so starting from nursery plants or rooted cuttings is far more reliable.

directions: Rockvine penstemon creeps over cliffs, ledges, and rock crevices at high elevation in the northern Rockies and Cascades, from Washington and Idaho into Montana, Alberta, and British Columbia. Its trailing, woody stems carry small glossy leaves that hug the rock face, and in late spring the plant is topped with disproportionately large, deep lavender to purple tubular flowers that draw hummingbirds and bumblebees. Give it a vertical or steeply sloped crevice with lean, mineral soil and essentially no standing moisture, since humid or soggy conditions quickly rot the crown. It is best suited to alpine troughs, tufa walls, and rock gardens in cool-summer climates rather than hot, humid lowland beds.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed experiences natural winter rains and chilling before spring growth; this chaparral native resents summer irrigation once dormant.

directions: Cleveland's beardtongue is a woody-based subshrub of the mountains and desert edges of San Diego County and northern Baja California, where it grows on dry scrub, chaparral, and pinyon-juniper slopes. Narrow gray-green leaves set off whorled clusters of vivid magenta-pink, lipped tubular flowers that are irresistible to hummingbirds and are among the showiest of any southwestern beardtongue. Plant it in fast-draining, mineral soil in full sun and withhold summer water once it is established, since this species evolved under a winter-rain, summer-drought regime. A light trim after bloom keeps the woody framework tidy and encourages the next season's flower spikes.

planting.note: Set out transplants in fall along the coast, or in spring inland, into sandy, well-drained soil under light forest cover; established plants tolerate occasional garden water if drainage is sharp.

directions: Rattan's beardtongue is an unusually shade-tolerant penstemon from the redwood and mixed conifer forests of coastal northern California, where it grows along partly shaded trail edges and sandy forest openings. Large clasping leaves rise on sturdy stems topped from April into midsummer by showy flowers ranging from pale lavender to deep red-violet, attracting bumblebees and hummingbirds in the dappled light. It prefers part shade and some summer moisture inland but accepts full sun with good drainage right along the coast. Use it under open-canopy trees or at the edge of a woodland border where most sun-loving xeric penstemons would struggle.

planting.note: Set transplants in spring into open woodland soil with some gravel content; seed benefits from a cold, moist stratification period before it will germinate reliably.

directions: Wilcox's beardtongue occupies open and lightly forested, often rocky ground from the foothills to mid-elevation mountains of eastern Washington and Oregon into Idaho and western Montana, a more shade-tolerant niche than most of its desert and alpine relatives. Glandular-hairy stems carry clusters of blue to bluish-purple flowers from late spring into midsummer, drawing bumblebees, hummingbirds, and a range of native pollinators. Grow it in gravelly, humus-light soil at a woodland edge or open pine savanna planting where it gets morning sun or dappled light rather than full, baking exposure. Because regional populations are uncommon and declining in parts of its range, source seed or plants only from reputable regional native-plant growers.
sources: Montana Natural Heritage Program Field Guide

planting.note: Plant container transplants in spring in rocky, fast-draining mountain soil in full sun; this species is adapted to dry summers at middle to high elevation and declines in heavy or constantly moist soils.

directions: San Gabriel beardtongue grows on dry, rocky slopes and open conifer forest of the Transverse and Peninsular Ranges of southern California, reaching south into Baja California. Its slender stems carry striking tubular flowers that shift from bright orange-red near the base to a paler, almost yellowish throat, a two-tone effect that makes it stand out among its red-flowered beardtongue relatives. It flowers in summer at the elevations where winter snow has recently melted, so it does best in a mountain or high-desert garden with cold winters and dry, sunny summers rather than a mild coastal setting. Plant in lean, rocky soil with excellent drainage and let it dry out between waterings once roots are established.

planting.note: Divide established clumps or set rooted cuttings in spring into gritty, sharply drained soil on an open, rocky slope; seed requires lengthy cold stratification and germinates slowly and unevenly.

directions: Snake River phlox is a regional endemic restricted to the dry, open basalt slopes and cliffs of Hells Canyon and the lower Salmon River canyon where Idaho, Oregon, and Washington meet. It forms a low, cushion-like mat of narrow leaves and produces an eye-catching spring display of flowers that range from white through pink to purple, often with several color forms on nearby plants in the wild. Because its native habitat is steep, rocky, and almost entirely rain-fed, it needs exceptionally sharp drainage and should be planted on a slope, raised bed, or scree garden rather than flat, moisture-retentive ground. It is an excellent choice for a dry rock garden in a region with cold winters and hot, dry summers that mimics its canyon-country origin.
sources: Idaho Department of Fish and Game

planting.note: Direct sow or set transplants in spring once soil has warmed, in gritty, fast-draining soil; this desert phlox needs warm, dry summer conditions to bloom well and resents heavy or constantly damp ground.

directions: Threadleaf phlox is one of the few phlox species built for heat, growing wild in the rocky foothills and canyons of the Chihuahuan Desert of West Texas and New Mexico. Thin, grass-like leaves line reddish stems that carry large, showy flowers in shades of pink, purple, yellow, or white, each marked with a distinctive pale throat that gives the plant its scientific name. Plant size and bloom vary considerably from year to year with rainfall, so give it gritty, mineral soil with excellent drainage and avoid rich garden beds or regular summer watering that softens its naturally tough constitution. It is a striking but somewhat exacting choice for a hot, sunny desert or xeriscape garden and is best grown from seed collected or sourced regionally, since nursery stock is uncommon.
sources: American Southwest (Wildflowers of the Southwest USA)
